Choosing an analysis for clustered binary outcomes when clusters are few and series are short: a simulation study and a clinical application

Abstract

Binary outcomes measured repeatedly on few subjects are analysed with generalized estimating equations (GEE), generalized linear mixed models or marginalized multilevel models. Small-sample corrections to the sandwich variance have been evaluated mainly by the number of clusters, with little attention to the number of measurement occasions. We compared eight analysis strategies over 1,896 simulated design points (10 to 145 clusters, 2 to 10 occasions, three data-generating mechanisms), including a scenario anchored to a neonatal lung-ultrasound cohort and four scenarios in which the latent variability grows strongly over time, and in subsamples of that cohort. The marginalized multilevel model was fitted with a convergence check that drops the time trend of the latent standard deviation when the fit reaches the boundary. With this check and a t reference distribution, it was the only strategy whose type I error was never clearly above 7.5% at any design point. With two or three occasions and up to 25 clusters no strategy was both available and calibrated. We recommend the marginalized model with the convergence check and a t reference, and GEE with the Fay-Graubard correction with a t reference as a simpler alternative.

Keywords. clustered binary data; few clusters; sandwich variance; small-sample correction; marginalized multilevel model; estimand; simulation study.

1. Introduction

Binary outcomes measured repeatedly within clusters, such as observations within patients or zones within a lung, are analysed in one of three ways. A generalized estimating equation (GEE) targets a population-averaged contrast and treats the dependence as a nuisance. A generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) targets a cluster-specific contrast and models the dependence explicitly. A marginalized multilevel model (MMM) specifies both: a marginal mean model of scientific interest and a conditional model that generates the dependence [1,2]. In applied work the choice usually follows the conventions of the field rather than evidence about the design at hand.

The three approaches target different quantities. Under a logit link the marginal and conditional contrasts differ. With a normal random intercept of variance \(\sigma^2\), the marginal contrast is approximately the conditional one multiplied by

\[\left(1 + k^2\sigma^2\right)^{-1/2}, \qquad k = \frac{16\sqrt{3}}{15\pi},\]

so the gap widens with the variance of the random effects [3,4]. A further difference arises when the two are adjusted for different covariate sets, because the odds ratio is not collapsible [5]. Method comparisons nevertheless often score a mixed model against a marginal target it does not estimate.

This paper concerns designs with few clusters and short series, where the asymptotic arguments behind all three approaches are weakest. Cluster-randomized trials with ten to thirty clusters are common. Among 100 reviewed trials, the 99 that reported the number of clusters had a median of 25 (interquartile range 15 to 44) [6], and 45% of stepped-wedge trials in another review had fewer than ten clusters [7]. Single-centre cohorts with two or three measurement occasions per subject are equally common in perinatal and paediatric research. The sandwich variance estimator is anticonservative with few clusters, and a family of small-sample corrections exists to repair it [8-10]. These corrections have been evaluated on subjects followed over time, with as few as ten subjects and four occasions [11-15]. They have also been evaluated on parallel cluster-randomized trials, where the simulation evidence has been reviewed systematically [16,17]. In the clustered designs of these evaluations, the unit within a cluster is a site within a mouth [8], a patient within a general practice [10], a participant within a cluster [16,18] or a youth within a community [19]. It is never a subject measured on several occasions. Cluster sizes range from 4 observations per cluster [19] to 150 on average [16]. None of these studies fits a random slope, and only [10] generates random regression coefficients, as a misspecification check. Whether their recommendations hold with two or three occasions per subject has not been established.

We report a simulation study planned and reported following Morris, White and Crowther [20], and a clinical application. The study has three components. The first is a simulation over three data-generating mechanisms and a grid that extends to ten clusters and two occasions. One scenario takes its prevalence and between-subject variance from a neonatal lung-ultrasound cohort. The second is a recommendation stated as a decision rule that must hold at every simulated design point, because an analyst knows the number of clusters and occasions but not the mechanism that generated the data. The third is a plasmode application, in which the cohort is repeatedly subsampled into the few-cluster regime with the full-cohort estimate as reference. Three results are established elsewhere and are cited rather than claimed here: the uncorrected sandwich is anticonservative with few clusters [8,9], the corrections trade level for power [16,21], and marginal and conditional estimands differ [5].

2. Methods

The study is reported in the order aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods and performance measures [20]. The revision reported here followed a protocol in this structure, versioned before any rerun and released with the code. Table 1 summarizes it. The full parameter table, extracted from the executed code, is in Table S1.

2.1 Aims

The aims concern the treatment-by-time interaction on the logit scale, in longitudinal binary data with few clusters and short series. We evaluated (i) the type I error of the test of no interaction; (ii) its power, raw and size-adjusted; (iii) bias, precision and confidence-interval coverage of the estimate against the estimand of each method; and (iv) the probability that a method returns a usable result. The clinical application and the decision rule of Section 2.6 build on these aims but are not simulation aims.

2.2 Data-generating mechanisms

The main grid crossed 16 cluster counts, N ∈ {10, 15, 20, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, 75, 85, 95, 105, 115, 125, 135, 145}, with 6 maximum numbers of occasions, T ∈ {2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10}. It also crossed five mean-model scenarios (M1-M5) and three mechanisms, giving 1,440 design points. Each design point was simulated under the alternative (H1) and the null (H0), and the two arms differed only in the tested coefficient. T is a maximum. Each subject was observed at all T occasions with probability 0.7, and otherwise at a number of occasions drawn uniformly from \(1\) to \(T-1\). At T = 2, between 29% and 31% of subjects therefore contributed a single observation. Treatment was assigned to subjects with probability 0.5.

The mean model of scenario M1 is \(\mathrm{logit}\,\mu = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \beta_2 \mathrm{trt} + \beta_3\, t \times \mathrm{trt}\). Its marginal coefficients under H1 are (-2, 0.1, 0.2, 0.2), which give a marginal prevalence of about 0.14 at T = 2. M2 adds a subject-level covariate (age). M3 and M4 add a random slope on time; in GenBinaryY its counterpart is a latent standard deviation that changes over time. M4 uses a smaller interaction (0.05). M5 adds a second covariate that varies over time (dose), with its own random slope.

The three mechanisms differ in how the dependence is generated.

  1. GenBinaryY is a marginalized model with a latent variable and a first-order transition term (R package MMLB) [1,2,22]. The latent standard deviation is a linear predictor, which in M3-M5 grows by 0.01 per occasion. This is the mechanism of the marginalized model.
  2. GLMM-native is a logistic mixed model with normal random effects. The random intercept has variance 1 and, in M3-M5, the random slope on time has variance 0.001. The conditional coefficients are the marginal ones multiplied by 1.16. This is the mechanism of the mixed model.
  3. GLMM-AR1 adds a latent first-order autoregressive process to the random effects of GLMM-native (ρ = 0.6, variance 0.5). Its conditional coefficients are calibrated on each replicate, so that the implied marginal coefficients equal the target. It is the mechanism of no method.

A sixth scenario, M1c, uses the mean model of M1 with the prevalence (0.59) and the between-subject variance (3.5) of the clinical cohort of Section 2.7. It covers 72 design points, with N up to 45 and T up to 6. Four further scenarios, M6 and M7 on GenBinaryY and on GLMM-native, test the convergence check of Section 2.4 where the latent variability grows strongly over time. In GenBinaryY the latent standard deviation grew by 0.1 or 0.25 per occasion; in GLMM-native the random-slope variance was 0.01 or 0.04. They cover the full grid (384 design points). With 10 occasions the latent standard deviation of GenBinaryY then grows from 1 to 1.9 or 3.25, against 1.09 in M3.

The values of the main scenarios were compared with the clinical cohort of Section 2.7. Their marginal prevalence (0.14 at T = 2 and 0.28 at T = 10 in M1) is much lower than in the cohort (0.59), and their random-intercept variance (1) is lower than the patient variance of the cohort (3.5); scenario M1c was added for this reason. The cohort has no treatment and few patients with repeated timepoints, so the interaction per occasion has no direct anchor in it. Its cumulative value at ten occasions (1.8 on the logit scale) is of the order of the regional contrasts estimated in the cohort, for example 1.1 between lateral and anterior zones. The autoregressive parameters of GLMM-AR1 were chosen to give a serial dependence that is detectable without dominating the cluster effect.

Each design point received 1,000 replicates per arm. In 44 design points, all in GLMM-AR1, only 971 to 999 datasets could be generated, because the per-replicate calibration met a singular system. Replicates in which one treatment arm was never observed after the first occasion were excluded from every denominator (247 per arm, the same in the three mechanisms). Replicate i of scenario m used the seed 20260805 + 1000m + i under the L’Ecuyer-CMRG generator. The seed was the same for both arms and for every N, T and mechanism, so the datasets are common random numbers across cells [20].

2.3 Estimands and true values

The estimand is the coefficient of the treatment-by-time interaction on the logit scale. It is marginal for the marginalized model, the GEEs and the shrinkage estimator, and conditional on the random effects for the mixed model. In GenBinaryY the marginal true value is the generating coefficient. There is no conditional true value, so bias and coverage of the mixed model are not defined on that mechanism. In GLMM-native the conditional true value is the generating coefficient. The marginal value was obtained by Gauss-Hermite quadrature on the realized design; under H0 it is not exactly zero, and it ranges from -0.0030 to -0.0011 across scenarios and T. In GLMM-AR1 the marginal true value is the target, and the conditional value was computed for each replicate.

2.4 Methods compared

Eight strategies were applied to every dataset (Table 1). The marginalized multilevel model was fitted with MMLB::mm (20 quadrature points), with the latent-variable and transition formulas of the GenBinaryY generator. GEEs with exchangeable working correlation were fitted with geepack [23]. They were combined with the uncorrected sandwich variance and with the corrections of Mancl and DeRouen [8], Kauermann and Carroll [9] and Fay and Graubard [10], computed by geesmv. Each correction ran under a hard time limit of 5 seconds, and a time-out counted as an unusable fit. The mixed model was fitted with lme4::glmer [24] (Laplace approximation). It had a random intercept in M1-M2 and the random slopes of the generating model in M3-M5. It was tested by Wald and by a likelihood-ratio test against the model without the interaction, with the same random effects. The shrinkage estimator rescales the mixed-model estimate and standard error by \((1 + k^2 D_{11})^{-1/2}\), with \(D_{11}\) the random-intercept variance. Its Wald statistic therefore equals that of the mixed model, and only its interval differs. Software versions are in Table S2.

MMLB::mm writes the latent standard deviation as \(\exp(a_0) + \exp(a_1)\,t\), so a slope of zero lies on the boundary of the parameter space. In the main scenarios with a latent standard deviation that changes over time (M3-M5), the generating slope is close to that boundary. In an earlier analysis of these data, two failure modes of the optimizer (nlm) produced excess rejections with long series: non-convergence with a shifted estimate, and convergence with a collapsed standard error. We therefore added a convergence check. A fit is declared at the boundary if nlm does not report convergence (return code other than 1 or 2) or if an estimated slope \(\exp(a_k)\) is below 0.001. Such a fit is replaced by the fit without the time trend of the latent standard deviation, and kept if that refit fails. The check was specified after the diagnosis and before the reanalysis of the 1,685,204 fits of M3-M5 that returned an estimate. Thresholds of 0.0001 and 0.01 were examined as sensitivity analyses, and scenarios M6-M7 were simulated afterwards to test the check. The marginalized model without the check is reported as a sensitivity analysis (Table S3).

Wald tests were referred to the standard normal in the primary tables and, as an alternative, to a t distribution with N - p degrees of freedom, p being the number of mean-model coefficients. The likelihood-ratio test was referred to a \(\chi^2\) distribution with one degree of freedom.

2.5 Performance measures

A replicate was usable for a Wald-based method when the fit returned without error and the estimate, its standard error and its p-value were finite, with |estimate| < 10 and \(0 <\) SE < 10. Fits that returned with warnings were kept; excluding them is a sensitivity analysis (Table S13). For the likelihood-ratio test, both nested fits had to return and the p-value had to be finite. The probability of a usable result was reported for every method and cell, with every attempted replicate in the denominator.

Type I error was the rejection rate at the nominal 5% under H0. Over the grid we report the pooled rate and two summaries computed within each mechanism. For each of the 16 cluster counts we took the departure from 5% of the replicate-weighted rate. The worst case is the largest of these departures, and the mean absolute departure is their mean. At each design point, a strategy was clearly above 7.5% when its rejection rate minus two Monte Carlo standard errors exceeded 7.5%. It was clearly below 2.5% when its rate plus two standard errors fell below 2.5%. These limits are Bradley’s liberal criterion [25]. Unconditional validity is the probability of a usable result multiplied by the probability of not rejecting a true null given one. Power was reported raw and size-adjusted. The size-adjusted critical value was the 95th percentile of |estimate/SE| over the usable null replicates of the same cell; for the likelihood-ratio test it was the 5th percentile of the null p-values. Bias, empirical and model-based standard errors, root mean squared error and coverage of the 95% interval were computed against the estimand of each method.

Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSE) were computed for every measure [20]. With 1,000 usable replicates, the MCSE of a rejection rate at 5% is 0.69 percentage points. This number of replicates was chosen so that a single cell resolves a departure from 5% of about 1.4 points. The datasets are common random numbers across cells. The MCSE of every summary over cells, and of every difference between methods, was therefore obtained by a bootstrap that resamples replicate indices jointly across all cells (2,000 resamples). A comparison between methods is written as a difference only when its bootstrap interval, the estimate ± 2 MCSE, lies entirely beyond a relevance margin fixed in advance. The margin is one percentage point for differences in type I error or coverage averaged over cells, 2.5 points for a single cell, and two points for differences in power. Intervals entirely within the margin are reported as similar. Intervals that straddle it are reported as differences of about the size of the margin. Counts of miscalibrated cells used exact binomial tests with the Benjamini-Hochberg and Benjamini-Yekutieli corrections. In the text, values are given to two significant figures. Tables give the digit that the MCSE supports, with the MCSE in the caption.

2.6 Decision rule

The recommendation of Figure 1 comes from a rule applied to every strategy, a strategy being a method with its reference distribution. A strategy was excluded if its type I error was clearly above 7.5% at any design point. Among the remaining strategies, the one that returned a usable result most often was recommended. The rule was applied to all 1,896 design points. It replaces the criterion of an earlier version of this work, which selected at each cluster count the method with the highest unconditional validity (Section 4.1).

2.7 Clinical application

The cohort comprises 207 neonates with ten lung-ultrasound zones scored at one to three timepoints. It gives 230 patient-timepoints and 2,296 zone-level outcomes; 22 patients contribute more than one timepoint. The outcome is severe loss of aeration (prevalence 0.59). In a logistic mixed model of the outcome on zone region with a patient random intercept, the patient variance is 3.5. Adding a patient-timepoint level drives the patient variance to the boundary and places a variance of 3.8 at the new level (likelihood-ratio \(\chi^2\) = 47 on one degree of freedom). The contrast of interest is posterior against anterior zones, adjusted for disease, invasive ventilation and gestational age. It was estimated by the marginalized model, the GEEs and the mixed model. With 207 clusters the cohort lies above the simulated range, so it was used as a plasmode. We drew 500 subsamples of whole patients at each of 10, 15, 20, 25 and 50 patients, with the full-cohort estimate of each method as its reference. Subsampling whole patients preserves the dependence structure exactly, and the covariate distribution only in expectation. Of the 25 patients ventilated invasively, a draw of 10 contains none with probability 0.27, and the mean model is then not identifiable.

3. Results

3.1 Type I error on the main grid

Table 2 gives the type I error of the eight methods on the 1,440 design points of the main grid, under a normal reference. The pooled rejection rate of the marginalized model with the convergence check ranged from 5.2% to 5.5% across mechanisms. It ranged from 5.3% to 5.8% for Fay-Graubard and from 5.5% to 6.1% for Mancl-DeRouen. On GenBinaryY it reached 13% for Kauermann-Carroll and 8.3% for the uncorrected GEE.

The marginalized model had the smallest worst-case departure from 5% on all three mechanisms: 0.83, 0.44 and 0.56 percentage points on GenBinaryY, GLMM-native and GLMM-AR1. Its lead over the next method was 2.8 points on GenBinaryY and about one point on the two random-effects mechanisms. Its mean absolute departure (0.24 to 0.54 points) and that of Fay-Graubard (0.52 to 1.0) were similar. On matched replicates usable for both methods, the two rejected a true null at similar rates.

Each method-cell was tested against 5% with the Benjamini-Hochberg correction within method. The marginalized model was detectably off nominal in 3% of its cells, Fay-Graubard in 23%, Mancl-DeRouen in 28% and Kauermann-Carroll in 87% (Table S5). The uncorrected GEE was above 5% by 19 points at N = 10 on GenBinaryY. Its smallest excess over the cluster counts was under half a point on every mechanism. Above 45 clusters, Fay-Graubard and the marginalized model were both within about half a point of 5% on the random-effects mechanisms.

The ordering of the methods was stable across mechanisms, with Spearman correlations of 0.90 to 0.98 between pairs of mechanisms. GLMM-AR1 differed from GLMM-native by 0.19 percentage points on average across methods. The mean absolute departure of the marginalized model fell from 1.5 points at two occasions to 0.71 at four or more (Table S4). At two occasions the five marginal methods departed by 1.5 to 2.5 points on average. The conditional methods departed by 5.6 (mixed model, Wald) to 11 points (shrinkage GLM).

3.2 The convergence check of the marginalized model

In scenarios M3-M5 the check replaced 68% of the fits of the marginalized model with the fit without the time trend of the latent standard deviation. Without the check, the marginalized model was clearly above 7.5% at 138 of the 864 null design points of these scenarios, 84 of them with eight or ten occasions. With the check it was clearly above 7.5% at 0. Its mean absolute departure at ten occasions fell from 2.8 to 0.67 points. Size-adjusted power at eight or ten occasions changed by 0.31 points on average. The thresholds 0.0001 and 0.01 in place of 0.001 changed the class of none of the 156 comparisons classified for this paper. With either threshold, the marginalized model with a t reference was not clearly above 7.5% at any design point.

In scenarios M6-M7 the fit without the time trend is misspecified. There the check intervened in 36% to 51% of fits under H0, and in 58% to 60% at two or three occasions, where nlm most often failed to converge. With a t reference, the marginalized model with the check was never clearly above 7.5% at the 384 design points. Under a normal reference its mean type I error was 5.2% to 5.8% across the four scenarios. Without the check, and with a t reference, it was clearly above 7.5% at 8 design points. Fay-Graubard with a t reference was clearly above 7.5% at 2 design points, all on GenBinaryY with the steeper slope (M7); its largest rate was 10% (Table S14).

3.3 Availability of a result

The probability of a usable result depended mostly on the number of occasions (Table 3). With random slopes and two occasions, the mixed model returned a usable Wald test in 0.002% of attempts. The likelihood-ratio test with the same random effects was usable in 0.14%, against 71% for the marginalized model and 73% for Fay-Graubard. With a random intercept only, the likelihood-ratio test was usable in 99% of attempts at two occasions, against 69% for the Wald test. From four occasions every method returned a usable result in more than 90% of attempts.

At 20 clusters or fewer, the likelihood-ratio test returned a usable result in 86% of attempts and the uncorrected GEE in 79%. The marginalized model (68%) and the three corrected sandwiches (each 69%) were similar. Unconditional validity ranged from 80% for the likelihood-ratio test to 61% for the Wald test of the mixed model.

3.4 Reference distribution and the decision rule

Referring the Wald statistic to a t distribution with N - p degrees of freedom lowered every pooled rejection rate. The shift was 0.53 to 1.1 percentage points over the grid and 1.4 to 3.7 points at 25 clusters or fewer (Table S11). Under the t reference the marginalized model became conservative at ten clusters. There it was clearly below 2.5% at 47 of 102 design points, against 18 for Fay-Graubard. Fay-Graubard also had the smaller worst-case departure under the t reference, 0.9 to 1.1 points against 3.0 to 3.4.

Table 4 applies the rule of Section 2.6 to the 1,896 design points of the main grid, M1c and M6-M7. The marginalized model with the check and a t reference was never clearly above 7.5%. Fay-Graubard with a t reference was clearly above 7.5% at 2 design points and Mancl-DeRouen with a t reference at 32. The likelihood-ratio test was clearly above 7.5% at 216 design points, and the Wald test of the mixed model with a t reference at 265. The recommended strategy returned a usable result in 91% of datasets, against 92% for Fay-Graubard with a t reference. It was clearly below 2.5% at 77 design points, against 116. With two or three occasions and at most 25 clusters, both returned a usable result in fewer than half of the datasets (40% and 44%). Both rejected a false null in fewer than 2% of attempted datasets.

3.5 Power and coverage

Raw power was highest for Kauermann-Carroll (35% on GenBinaryY), which was also the most anticonservative method. The ordering by raw power did not survive size adjustment (Table 5). After size adjustment, power ranged from 21% to 27% across methods and mechanisms. On GenBinaryY the Wald test of the mixed model had more size-adjusted power than Fay-Graubard, by 2.2 points with the default optimizer of lme4 and by 3.1 points with bobyqa. On GLMM-AR1 the difference was about two points with the default optimizer, and the two were similar with bobyqa. On GLMM-native the two were similar with the default optimizer, and with bobyqa Fay-Graubard had more power, by about two points.

Coverage of the 95% interval was 94% to 95% for Fay-Graubard, Mancl-DeRouen and the marginalized model on every mechanism (Table S12). It was furthest from nominal for Kauermann-Carroll, at 86% to 89%.

3.6 Scenario anchored to the cohort

Scenario M1c has the prevalence and between-subject variance of the cohort (72 design points). Two results of the main grid did not hold there. Under a normal reference the marginalized model rejected a true null in 6.8% to 7.0% of usable replicates, against 5.0% to 5.1% for Fay-Graubard. Its worst-case departure was larger than that of the best method by about one to two points. Under a t reference its rate was 5.0% to 5.1%, and that of Fay-Graubard 3.5% to 3.6%. The size-adjusted power of the Wald test of the mixed model fell below that of Fay-Graubard, by 4.3 to 4.9 points with the default optimizer. With bobyqa the deficit was about two points on GenBinaryY and GLMM-AR1, and the two were similar on GLMM-native. The default optimizer returned degenerate fits with a near-zero standard error. Which method had the fewest or the most miscalibrated cells could not be distinguished in M1c.

3.7 Clinical application

In the full cohort the posterior-versus-anterior contrast was 0.38 (SE 0.17) by the marginalized model and 0.38 by GEE. The mixed model gave 0.48 (SE 0.12) on its conditional scale. In subsamples of 10 patients, 22% of draws contained no invasively ventilated patient, so that the mean model could not be fitted (Table S15). Among the fits that were returned, a usable result was obtained by the mixed model in 100%, by the marginalized model in 100% and by the uncorrected GEE in 92%. It was obtained by Fay-Graubard in 45% and by Mancl-DeRouen in 20%; most failures of the corrections returned a point estimate without a standard error. Across subsample sizes, the standard error of the mixed model was 0.53 to 0.65 times the empirical standard deviation of its estimates. The corresponding ratio was 0.87 to 1.1 for the marginalized model. The bias of the marginalized model against its full-cohort estimate fell from 0.16 at 10 patients to 0.015 at 50.

4. Discussion

4.1 The recommendation

The rule of Section 2.6 selects the marginalized multilevel model with the convergence check and a t reference with N - p degrees of freedom, at every number of clusters and occasions (Figure 1). Across the 1,896 simulated design points it was the only strategy whose type I error was never clearly above 7.5%. It returned a usable result in 91% of datasets. Fay-Graubard with a t reference returned a usable result about as often and needs no convergence check, so it is a reasonable alternative. It was clearly above 7.5% only with at most 25 clusters and a latent variability that grows steeply over time. The two strategies are conservative in different places: the marginalized model at ten clusters, Fay-Graubard more often elsewhere (Table 4).

The rule asks that a recommendation hold at every design point, because an analyst knows the number of clusters and occasions but not the mechanism that generated the data. It replaces a criterion that maximized unconditional validity at each cluster count. That criterion rewards a method for answering, whatever its level. On the present data it would have recommended the likelihood-ratio test of the mixed model up to 25 clusters, a test that was clearly above 7.5% at 216 design points. The change of criterion also reverses the general recommendation of the earlier version, which was Fay-Graubard. The reason is that scenarios M6-M7 exposed design points at which Fay-Graubard with a t reference was clearly above 7.5%.

With two or three occasions and up to 25 clusters, no strategy was both available and calibrated. The recommended strategy and Fay-Graubard returned a usable result in fewer than half of the datasets and almost never detected the simulated effect. With a random slope and two occasions, the random-effects covariance of the mixed model is not identifiable, since two subject-level parameters saturate two observations, and its Wald test was essentially never usable. The case for the maximal random-effects structure [26] is thus bounded by power [27] and, with two occasions, by identifiability. In this corner the design determines what can be learned more than the analysis does. Four or more occasions per subject, or more clusters, should be planned where possible.

4.2 The convergence check

The check addresses a property of the parametrization rather than of the marginalized model. MMLB::mm writes the latent standard deviation with an exponentiated slope, so a slope near zero lies on the boundary of the parameter space, and in all the main scenarios the generating slope was close to zero. At the boundary nlm either stopped without converging, with an estimate shifted by an amount that did not shrink with the standard error, or converged with a collapsed standard error. Both failures produced excess rejections that grew with the number of clusters and occasions. This is why the marginalized model appeared miscalibrated with long series in an earlier analysis. Replacing such fits with the fit without the time trend removed the excess. The check intervened far more often than we had anticipated, mainly because nlm failed to converge with two or three occasions or few clusters. Where it intervened, the type I error stayed close to nominal. It also remained calibrated in M6-M7, where the fit without the time trend is misspecified. Analysts who use the marginalized model with a latent standard deviation that changes over time should apply the check and report how often it intervened.

4.3 Relation to previous work

We reproduce the anticonservatism of the uncorrected sandwich with few clusters [8,9]. Li and Redden found that Kauermann-Carroll attains the nominal level at ten clusters under a t reference [16]. In our data its rate at ten clusters was 3.9% to 5.5%. Over the whole grid, however, it was clearly above 7.5% at 951 of 1,896 design points, so the finding does not extend beyond the cluster range in which it was established. Mancl and DeRouen reported sizes close to nominal with ten subjects [8], and Bie et al. favoured GEE with their correction [18]. Under a t reference its pooled rate was 4.7% to 5.3%, inside their band. It was nevertheless clearly above 7.5% at 32 design points, 18 of them in scenarios M6-M7. The marginalized model has been studied for moderate to long series [22], and the short series studied here complement that work. Estimation methods for mixed logistic models with few clusters are reviewed by McNeish [28].

4.4 Limitations

In the main scenarios the random-slope variance and the time trend of the latent standard deviation were small. Conclusions about random slopes therefore rest mainly on scenarios M6-M7, which cover one structure (a slope on time) and two mechanisms. The working correlation of the GEEs was exchangeable throughout, and misspecified working correlations were not simulated. The degrees of freedom of the t reference were N - p and were not varied, whereas Li and Redden used K - 2 [16]. GLMM-AR1 behaved almost exactly like GLMM-native, so the study rests on two distinct mechanisms. Each of these is the home model of one method: GenBinaryY of the marginalized model and GLMM-native of the mixed model. In GLMM-native the marginal value under the null is not exactly zero. It ranges from -0.0030 to -0.0011 in the main scenarios and reaches -0.0079 in M6-M7. The convergence check was introduced after part of the results had been seen, and was then tested on scenarios simulated afterwards. Small-sample corrections were computed with geesmv, whose numerical failures at small samples are documented in Section S4. An independent implementation, such as the CR2 estimator of clubSandwich [29,30], would avoid them. The clinical application uses one cohort and one outcome. The subsampling resamples whole patients, and the patient-timepoint level that carries most of the dependence is identified by only 22 patients measured more than once.

5. Conclusions

With few clusters and short series, the choice of analysis for a clustered binary outcome decides whether the test keeps its nominal level and whether it returns an answer at all. The marginalized multilevel model was the only strategy that kept its level at every simulated design point, provided that it was fitted with a check that drops the time trend of the latent standard deviation at the boundary and referred to a t distribution. With two or three occasions and up to 25 clusters, no strategy was both available and calibrated, so in that regime the design limits what any analysis can show.

We recommend the marginalized model with the convergence check and a t reference. GEE with the Fay-Graubard correction with a t reference is a simpler alternative, to be used with caution when clusters are few and the between-subject variability grows over time.

Code and data availability

The simulation code, the per-replicate results and the scripts that produce every number, table and figure of this paper are available at https://github.com/lucavd/MMM (commit f9ab317). They will be archived on Zenodo with a DOI at submission. The manuscript source reads every number in the text from a registry of values, each with its source file and checksum. The clinical cohort cannot be shared publicly; the plasmode results are included as summary tables.

Aims Type I error and power of the test of no treatment-by-time interaction, bias and coverage of its estimate, and probability of a usable result, with few clusters and short series
Data-generating mechanisms GenBinaryY (marginalized latent-variable transition model), GLMM-native (logistic mixed model), GLMM-AR1 (mixed model with latent first-order autoregression); scenarios M1-M5 on the full grid of 16 cluster counts (10 to 145) and 6 series lengths (2 to 10), 1,440 design points; M1c anchored to the clinical cohort (72 design points); M6-M7 with a steep time trend of the latent variability (384 design points); null and alternative arm for each, 1,000 replicates per arm
Estimands Interaction coefficient on the logit scale: marginal (marginalized model, GEEs, shrinkage GLM) or conditional on the random effects (GLMM)
Methods Marginalized multilevel model (MMLB::mm) with convergence check; GEE with uncorrected sandwich and with the Mancl-DeRouen, Kauermann-Carroll and Fay-Graubard corrections (geepack, geesmv); GLMM with Wald and likelihood-ratio tests (lme4); shrinkage-rescaled GLMM. Wald tests with normal and t (N - p degrees of freedom) reference
Performance measures Probability of a usable result; type I error (pooled, worst case and mean absolute departure over cluster counts, clearly above 7.5% or below 2.5% per design point); raw and size-adjusted power; bias, empirical and model standard error, coverage; Monte Carlo standard errors by block bootstrap over replicates
